claims.text: At 600–800°C, the wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings is governed primarily by rapid formation of a continuous protective oxide scale at the wear interface.
The protective oxide scale is particularly rich in Cr and Cu oxides.
The oxide scale reduces asperity contact at the sliding interface.
The oxide scale dissipates mechanical energy during wear.
A preformed oxide scale lowers wear relative to coatings without such a preformed scale.
The baseline FeNiCrCoCu coating has a homogeneous nanocrystalline microstructure.
The baseline as-deposited coating has minimal pre-existing oxide.
Pre-oxidation at 600–700°C in an oxygen-containing atmosphere promotes formation of a protective oxide layer before wear testing.
Because the coating remains thin, coating–substrate interactions are significant during high-temperature wear.
Oxide-scale continuity, thickness, and composition mediate the coating's wear response.
A continuous oxide layer reduces metal-to-metal contact.
A continuous oxide layer suppresses micro-fracture propagation.
Thermally accelerated oxidation of FeNiCrCoCu produces a self-forming, adherent surface scale.
The oxide scale functions as a low-shear barrier during sliding.
The oxide barrier mitigates plastic deformation and abrasive wear.
Pre-oxidized coatings will have lower wear-track depth than as-deposited coatings tested under identical high-temperature conditions.
Pre-oxidized coatings will have lower friction coefficients than as-deposited coatings tested under identical high-temperature conditions.
Improved wear performance will correlate with the presence of a coherent oxide layer.
The proposed mechanism is limited to thin FeNiCrCoCu protective coatings under 600–800°C sliding or abrasive wear in an oxidizing environment.
Failure of pre-oxidation to produce a statistically significant wear reduction, or observation of worse wear, would falsify the proposed beneficial oxide-scale mechanism.
